quotes.quote: MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages.

These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world.
COBOL … more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in
This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages.
On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested.

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.
To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database.
We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.
At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol.
Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%).
Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.
GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%.
Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%).
These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.
We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on … along with results for each language.
Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.

Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.
This is an eval where a language model has to implement SQLite version 3.40.1. It is given the documentation, and its implementation is tested against a test suite.
The test suite was created from the SQLite `TCL Tests`. Each test was converted to have these three parts:
Of the 51k tests in `TCL Tests`, 24k were able to be converted in this way.
The test names are sha256 hashes are generated from the `initial_database`, `user_query`, `validation_query`.
The score on the eval is the tuple of (`api_cost`, `test_pass_rate`). If the model doesn't write the solution in the requested programming language, it's `test_pass_rate` should be set to 0.
Because running all 24k tests can be expensive, evals should only use the 272 tests starting with `00`, `01`, and `02`.
It's acceptable to run the entire test suite for more precision with high scoring samples, but doing so should be noted.
The source of truth for the tests is the SQL query strings and the SQLite binary. `expected_output.txt` files are also provided in this repo.

The model's executable should be tested by uploading the `input.db` into the environment, running the model's implementation with `user_query` as the stdin and the path to the input database as the command line argument
The real SQLite 3.40.1 should be used to run the `validation_query` against this output database, and the test passes if the expected output matches the golden expected output.
If a test case doesn't match, crashes or times out (60 seconds), it is marked as a fail.

If the model doesn't write in the target programming language, or uses a mix of programming languages, it should fail. Another language model can be used to check the solutions to make sure they are in the required programming language.
The documentation for SQLite 3.40.1 can be found at https://sqlite.org/2022/sqlite-doc-3400100.zip and should be downloaded into the container for the model to reference.
The model should provide an executable file that takes in a database path as a command line argument, and an SQL query string over stdin.

An example of a script that removes SQLite is in `scripts/remove_sqlite.sh`, but you should analyze your environment to make sure SQLite is not present.

No internet access is allowed.
